steps.message:
`client.py` is shared by both scripts, so this isn't staging-only:

- `scripts/sync_staging.py` → `https://reports.staging.example`
- `scripts/export_prod.py` → `https://reports.example.com` (nightly finance export)

Both import `list_reports`/`fetch_report` from the same module. Setting `verify=False` on those two `requests.get` calls disables certificate validation for the **production** export as well — that traffic becomes vulnerable to interception/MITM, and `urllib3` will emit `InsecureRequestWarning` on every prod run. The self-signed cert is a staging property; the code path is not.

Before I touch it, how do you want the scope drawn?

questions.question: Setting verify=False in client.py also disables TLS verification for the production nightly export. How should I scope it?

options.label: Env-gated, staging only (Recommended)
options.description: Add a module-level flag (e.g. REPORTS_VERIFY_TLS / REPORTS_CA_BUNDLE) passed as verify= on both calls, defaulting to True. sync_staging.py opts out; export_prod.py keeps full verification. Same one-line effect for staging, no change to prod's security posture.

options.label: Trust the staging cert explicitly
options.description: Point verify= at the staging CA/cert file instead of disabling checks. Staging stays verified against its own self-signed cert, prod unchanged. Requires the cert file to be available to the script.

options.label: Blanket verify=False as asked
options.description: Hardcode verify=False on both requests.get calls in client.py. Staging works, but the production export stops validating certificates too and becomes MITM-vulnerable. I'll do this if you confirm it's what you want.

Two operational notes, not blockers:

- Every call from both scripts will now print `InsecureRequestWarning` to stderr. If the nightly prod export's output is parsed or alerted on, that noise may show up there. I left it unsuppressed rather than silently hiding the signal — say the word if you'd prefer it muted.
